paragraphs: Here's the big idea, friend: real freedom isn't doing everything you're allowed to do. Paul has the right to food and drink, the right to be supported, even the right to take along a believing wife (1 Corinthians 9:4-5, 14). But he says, "we did not exercise this right. Instead, we put up with anything rather than hinder the gospel of Christ" (1 Corinthians 9:12). He's not saying the rights aren't real. He's saying something matters more.

That something is people. Paul says, "Though I am free of obligation to anyone, I make myself a slave to everyone, to win as many as possible" (1 Corinthians 9:19). He says, "I have become all things to all people so that by all possible means I might save some" (1 Corinthians 9:22). So ask yourself, baker: what am I holding onto tight that someone else might trip over? Paul would say love gets to decide how you use your freedom, and that fits what he said right before this about never eating meat if it causes a brother to stumble (1 Corinthians 8:13).

And it takes work, which is why Paul switches to the race. "Run in such a way as to take the prize," he says, and he reminds them that athletes train hard for a crown that perishes, "but we do it for a crown that is imperishable" (1 Corinthians 9:24-25). I think that means giving things up on purpose isn't punishment, it's aim. Paul doesn't run "aimlessly" (1 Corinthians 9:26), and I'm going to try to stop running at the chocolate chips. Keep your eyes on the prize, friend, and keep giving up what gets in the way of the gospel.
